etymologies.etymologyHTML: Late 14th century, as Middle English attempten, from Old French atempter, from Latin attemptō (“I try, solicit”), from ad (“to”) + temptare, more correctly tentare (“to try”); see tempt. The noun is from the 1530s, the sense "an assault on somebody's life, assassination attempt" (French attentat) is from 1580.

quote.citation: 1842, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, The Village Blacksmith:
quote.text: Something attempted, something done, / Has earned a night's repose.

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Sarah Glaz, “Ode to Prime Numbers”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 4:
quote.text: Some poems, echoing the purpose of early poetic treatises on scientific principles, attempt to elucidate the mathematical concepts that underlie prime numbers. Others play with primes’ cultural associations. Still others derive their structure from mathematical patterns involving primes.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To try to move, by entreaty, by afflictions, or by temptations; to tempt.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Yet since I see you fearful, that neither my coat, integrity, nor persuasion can with ease attempt you, I will go further than I meant, to pluck all fears out of you.

quote.citation: 1859, Alfred Tennyson, “Vivien”, in Idylls of the King, London: Edward Moxon & Co., […], →OCLC, page 102:
quote.text: It made the laughter of an afternoon / That Vivien should attempt the blameless king.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To try to win, subdue, or overcome.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: Dear sir, of force I must attempt you further: / Take some remembrance of us, as a tribute.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To attack; to make an effort or attack upon; to try to take by force.

quote.citation: 1830, John Motley, The Rise of the Dutch Republic:

definitions.definition: The action of trying at something. [1530]

quote.citation: 2012 March, William E. Carter, Merri Sue Carter, “The British Longitude Act Reconsidered”, in American Scientist‎[1], volume 100, number 2, page 87:
quote.text: But was it responsible governance to pass the Longitude Act without other efforts to protect British seamen? Or might it have been subterfuge—a disingenuous attempt to shift attention away from the realities of their life at sea

definitions.definition: An assault or attack, especially an assassination attempt. [1580]

quote.citation: 1584, Allen’s Defence Of English Catholics, cited after Edinburgh Review 1883, page 378:
quote.text: No man can charge us of any attempt against the realm.
